research_text:
## 1. API and finding

`javax.crypto.Cipher` provides encryption, decryption, key wrapping and key unwrapping. An application obtains a cipher for a *transformation* and initializes it for an operation with a key or certificate, optionally supplying parameters and randomness. Oracle documents the API at https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

For the reported key-origin finding, the relevant value is the **`key` argument bound by a modeled `init` event**. The CrySL rule requires one of three predicates for that value: `generatedKey`, `generatedPubkey`, or `generatedPrivkey`. These are rule-analysis predicates, not Java API properties or exceptions. The message alone does not establish the key’s actual origin or why the analyzer did not accept it. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

## 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

- **Transformation and initialization:** Oracle recommends specifying the algorithm, mode and padding rather than relying on provider defaults. Initialize the cipher with a key and parameters appropriate to the chosen transformation and operation. Inappropriate keys or parameters can cause initialization exceptions. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
- **Key provenance:** Oracle documents `KeyGenerator` for generating symmetric keys and `KeyStore` for storing keys. It also permits constructing a `SecretKey` from raw bytes with `SecretKeySpec`; that constructor does not validate that the bytes form a suitable key for the named algorithm. Oracle’s API does **not** prescribe a universal replacement for a key rejected by the CrySL predicate. A rule-predicate failure is not, by itself, proof that a Java key is invalid. Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Authentication and nonce lifecycle:** Oracle’s GCM example uses `AES/GCM/NoPadding`, supplies any AAD before data processing, and reinitializes with a different IV for each encryption under the same key. AEAD decryption verifies the tag. A transformation-only change does not address reuse of an already initialized cipher or its IV. Do not introduce a constant key, IV or nonce. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
- **Parameters:** For applicable `init` overloads, a provider may generate required encryption parameters; Oracle documents retrieving them with `getParameters()` or `getIV()`. Decryption requires the appropriate parameters. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

## 3. Compatibility and migration

Oracle’s GCM example requires the same key, GCM parameters and AAD for decryption; the API documents that the authentication tag is appended to ciphertext on encryption and verified on decryption. **Consequently, changing a key, transformation or parameters can affect readers of persisted data and wire messages.** The cited API does not define a general persisted or wire envelope, versioning scheme, or migration procedure. Retaining the ability to read old data depends on the existing format and availability of its original key and parameters; those details were not supplied. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

Platform support is version- and provider-dependent:

- Java SE 8 documents GCM usage but does **not** list AES/GCM among its mandatory `Cipher` transformations. `GCMParameterSpec` has existed since Java 7. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))
- Java SE 17 requires AES/GCM/NoPadding with 128-bit keys; Java SE 26 lists both 128- and 256-bit AES/GCM. Check the target implementation for additional support and tag-length constraints. Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/Cipher.html; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

## 4. Exact CrySL matching declarations

The supplied source is https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl. It declares `SPEC javax.crypto.Cipher`. Its relevant `init` event declarations and key requirement are, verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

```text
	i1: init(encmode, certificate);
	i2: init(encmode, certificate, random);
	i3: init(encmode, key);
	i4: init(encmode, key, paramSpec);
	i5: init(encmode, key, params);
	i6: init(encmode, key, paramSpec, random);
	i7: init(encmode, key, params, random);
	i8: init(encmode, key, random);
```

```text
	generatedKey[key, alg(transformation)] || generatedPubkey[key] || generatedPrivkey[key];
```

The source declares the parameter objects’ types, including `java.security.Key`, `Certificate`, `AlgorithmParameterSpec`, `AlgorithmParameters`, and `SecureRandom`. Thus, its event patterns specify **parameter lists**, not an unrestricted match on every method named `init`. The predicate evaluates alternatives for the bound key; the symmetric-key alternative also refers to the transformation’s algorithm. The other event names declared in the file are `getInstance`, `update`, `updateAAD`, `doFinal`, and `wrap`, each with listed parameter patterns. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

**A method merely sharing one of those names on an unrelated API is not specified as a match by this Cipher-scoped rule.** The file itself does not document an analyzer’s implementation of receiver resolution or rule matching, so it cannot establish how a particular detector handles an unrelated same-name call. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

## Source limits

The rule URL points to a moving branch. The supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified here, and the detector version, compiled rule artifact, analysis configuration and actual key flow were not supplied. The source therefore does not establish the precise cause of this particular reported `UnsatisfiedConstraint`, nor does it document a repository-specific migration path.
